rock_grade: Mostly 3rd-4th class with low-5th summit blocks; one short, hard boulder-style move (5.7-5.9) on Dorado Needle
overview: A glaciated high traverse through the heart of the North Cascades that links five of the range's big summits: Eldorado Peak, Dorado Needle, Klawatti Peak, Austera Peak and Primus Peak. This version starts and ends at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on the Cascade River Road, crossing the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers out to Primus and back. It is serious, committing terrain: crevassed ice, steep snow, moats and short, exposed rock summit blocks, far from any easy exit.
beta: From high camp on the edge of the Inspiration Glacier, the peaks can be taken in any order, but a common plan is Eldorado first (a short climb up the snow of its East Ridge to an exposed, knife-edge snow crest at the summit), then east across the Inspiration Glacier to camp at the rock col on the south side of Klawatti. From there, continue over the Klawatti Glacier and the North Klawatti Glacier to Primus, whose south side is easy snow, slabs and mostly stable talus, reaching the south ridge a
breakdown: Eldorado Glacier to high camp: Glacier
Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti col: Glacier
Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers to Primus: Glacier
McAllister Glacier to Dorado Needle: Glacier

first_pass.evidence: Dorado Needle summit block lost a piece to rockfall; one party reports a short 5.7-5.9 crux there, another says it is 'definitely not 5.7'; older reports call Dorado's NW ridge 5.3 / low 5th; Austera has a couple of 5th-class moves.
first_pass.note: Crux grade is disputed after the block collapse; reports range from 5.3 to 5.9.

face: North Face — Middle Finger Buttress (right side)
overview: A III, 5.9 line up the north face just east of Middle Finger Buttress, following obvious crack systems up good rock to a finishing overhanging off-width crack.
beta: Grade III, 5.9. Lies just east of Middle Finger Buttress on the peak's broad north face; climbs a line on the right side, with obvious cracks leading up the center on good rock, finishing with an overhanging off-width crack.

first_pass.evidence: No online source found for a 'North Buttress' (III 5.9) on Amphitheater Mountain; Mountain Project lists only MFB Left/Right, North Ridge, Finger of Fatwa and Pilgrimage to Mecca. Grade kept from the record.
The Amphitheater (Cape Disappointment) on Mountain Project lists 4 climbs and describes gullies used as 3rd-class access/descent; the individual route grade was not visible.

overview: Anderson's Thumb is a sharp rock spire on the Mount Anderson massif in the central Olympics, near Echo Rock and Flypaper Pass. Reaching it requires a long approach and glacier travel on the Eel Glacier - the Anderson Glacier on the south side of the massif disappeared by roughly 2011 and is now bare rock/moraine rather than crevassed ice. The spire itself is exposed Class 4 to low-5th-class climbing on good Olympic sandstone - a small but committing technical summit.
beta: Anderson's Thumb has no dedicated published route description or topo. The only documented accounts are trip-report asides from parties climbing Mount Anderson: one pair was tempted to scramble it on their way out from the Anderson Glacier moraine and judged it an enjoyable rock climb on good sandstone — notably solid rock compared with the loose, meta-sedimentary terrain elsewhere on the massif — but turned back when heavy rain began. first_pass.evidence: Anderson's Thumb (~6,850 ft subpeak of Mount Anderson) is described only as 'a fun rock climb on good sandstone'; no numeric grade found online. Record says Class 4 / low 5th.
first_pass.note: Low 5th with no number anywhere, so 5.0 per rule.

face: Southwest ridge / summit tower above the McAllister Glacier
fa: Peak first ascent: September 16, 1965 by Joe and Joan Firey, John and Irene Meulemans, and Anthony Hovey. Specific route first ascent unknown.
overview: A remote summit on the high glacier divide near Primus and the head of the McAllister Glacier, Austera Peak is one of the wilder objectives in the Eldorado high country. It is typically reached on multi-day glacier traverses by parties seeking solitude and serious alpine terrain.
beta: This is the standard route to Austera Peak, involving glacier travel through some of the most scenic terrain in the North Cascades. From Eldorado Camp, rope up early and traverse multiple glaciers, passing two major cols (one technical) before reaching the summit tower. Most of the route is scrambling and glacier travel with only minimal technical rock climbing.

first_pass.evidence: Beckey calls the SW ridge 3rd class, but glacial recession now leaves a low-5th pitch at its base; summit tower low 5th (chockstone 5.2).
first_pass.note: Record headline says Grade II but commitment says III; Mountain Project gives the Austera glacier route Grade III.

face: South/southeast side (Diobsud Creek Glacier flank), with the Green Lake Glacier on the northeast side used for descent or as a link on longer traverses
overview: Bacon Peak carries a small icecap divided into three named glaciers — Diobsud Creek (SE), Green Lake (NE), and Noisy Creek (NW) — high above the Baker Lake / Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness country. The standard climb approaches via the Anderson & Watson Lakes Trailhead (or a shorter, brushier route from Bacon Creek Road), climbs a steep gully to the Diobsud Creek Glacier, ropes up for the icecap, and finishes with a short Class 2-3 scramble to the rocky summit.
beta: This is a committing multi-day alpine objective requiring glacier travel, crevasse rescue skills, and strong route-finding ability. The route is accessed via heavily forested terrain with significant deadfall obstacles, followed by steep snow and glacier travel to a 6,250 ft saddle camp. The final summit push is relatively short from camp but requires careful navigation in potentially whiteout conditions. first_pass.evidence: Non-technical, low-angle icecap glacier (Diobsud Creek Glacier descends 7,000 to 6,000 ft over ~1 mi); approach is steep brush and loose dirt gullies; no source gives a class rating.
first_pass.note: Default Class 2 for a non-technical glacier climb; alpine_grade II and commitment III disagree.

overview: A ~3,000-ft low-angle sandstone slab climbs the SE shoulder of Bears Breast from Shovel Creek to ~6,700 ft, followed by ~600 ft of exposed scrambling and one short, loose pitch to the summit block — one of the longest continuous slabs in the Cascades.
beta: A long, remote slab route up the SE shoulder. Reached via a multi-day approach up the Waptus River and Shovel Creek drainages, the ~3,000-ft slab itself is low-angle and mostly climbed unroped, topped by a further ~600 ft of exposed scrambling and one short, loose final pitch to the true summit.
breakdown: Slab base to south shoulder: Low 5th (unrated friction)
Summit block scramble: Class 3-4 / exposed scramble

first_pass.evidence: The slab itself is unrated easy friction ('only using our hands in a few spots'); the finish is via the summit block, which the two Mega Slab routes on Mountain Project and the SW Face reports grade 5.6. One party called its summit chimney 'pretty easy but exposed'.
first_pass.note: Grade is the summit block's; the slab alone is low 5th or less.

fa: Forest Farr and Art Winder, July 19, 1931 — this was the first ascent of Big Four Mountain overall, made via the northwest ridge.
overview: The historic original line to Big Four's summit, first climbed in 1931. Modern trip-report literature on Big Four is dominated by the Dry Creek, Tower, and Spindrift Couloir lines, so detailed contemporary route-finding notes for this specific ridge are sparse compared to those routes.
beta: Big Four Mountain's first ascent was made July 19, 1931 by Forest Farr and Art Winder via the northwest ridge -- the original route to the summit. As with the mountain's other lines, this route begins from the Big Four viewpoint/ice caves trail approach on the Mountain Loop Highway.

first_pass.evidence: First ascent route (Farr and Winder, July 1931); no online source gives a class for the northwest ridge. The easiest route on the peak is class 3-4, so this ridge is at least that.
first_pass.note: No source rates this ridge; Class 4 is an estimate.

fa: Ben Guydelkon and Ron Miller, July 25, 1972
overview: A technical rock-and-snow line on the mountain's north side/NE ridge that climbs a prominent gully to the first of three rock towers, works over and between the towers via rock climbing and a rappel into a notch, then finishes up a long, steep, exposed snowfield to the summit.
beta: First climbed July 25, 1972 by Ben Guydelkon and Ron Miller as a new line on Big Four's north side. From the end of the ice-caves trail, the party traversed to the northeast side of the first tower to a prominent gully; climbing this gully let them work west onto and up the first tower. They rappelled into a notch, climbed two more towers, then finished with rock scrambling leading to a long, steep, exposed snowfield to the summit.

first_pass.evidence: Tower Route on the NE ridge described as a hard rock route; a Direct Tower Route TR lists a 5.7 bolted slab and pitches to 5.8 (direct variant)
first_pass.note: Little published detail; a direct variant reportedly has 5.8 pitches.

fa: Jeff Dial and Don Williamson, May 11, 1971
overview: A 10-pitch granite line up the crest of Big Snow Mountain's East Buttress above Hardscrabble Lake, first climbed with aid at NCCS III, 5.7, A1 in 1971 and later freed at 5.10 by Pete Doorish. A rarely repeated, semi-obscure Cascades classic on notably sound rock.
beta: From lower Hardscrabble Lake, traverse its left (north) side and scramble over two rock bands to reach the south side of the buttress at about 5,400 ft. Climb close to the crest of the buttress, working under overhangs, on generally solid granite for 10 pitches (originally 4 pitches of class 4 followed by class 5 climbing with occasional aid pitons) to the summit area.

first_pass.evidence: 1971 FA III 5.7 with aid; a Doorish route on the buttress has gone free at 5.10

fa: Dan Davis and John Holland, August 22, 1964
overview: A rarely-repeated alpine rock route up the prominent central rib of Booker's 3,000+ foot Northeast Face, one of the steepest walls in Washington, first climbed via an icefall approach and a crumbly mid-face rock band to a notch just below the summit.
beta: From a camp near the head of Park Creek, climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, then go left up the glacier to an icefall and traverse right through and under it (reported as a genuinely exposed, 'frightening' crossing) to reach the main rock wall. Follow a prominent central rib essentially straight up the face on generally sound Cascade granodiorite/orthogneiss, through a crumbly red rock stratum that crosses the whole face at roughly mid-height, to a 100-foot notch nea

first_pass.evidence: FA report: NCCS IV, F8; mostly class 4 and 5, plus very steep snow/ice at the notch
first_pass.note: F8 mapped to 5.8; the notch also needed very steep snow and ice.

face: Northwest side, accessed via the Booker-Buckner col
overview: An alternate Class 3 scramble reached from Park Creek Pass via the Booker-Buckner col, on the mountain's northwest side; used mainly by parties already in the Park Creek/Buckner area on a multi-day traverse rather than as a dedicated approach.
beta: From a camp at or near Park Creek Pass, ascend toward the Booker-Buckner col, crossing a broad sandy gully around 6,900 ft roughly a mile from the pass; a few crevasses/cracks near the col are typically bypassed on snowbridges. From the col, the northwest side of Booker is mostly Class 3 scrambling with some easy Class 2-3 terrain to the summit.

first_pass.evidence: Route on Booker from the Booker-Buckner col described as class 3 with tricky route finding; the col itself is steep hard snow

overview: Buckskin Mountain (~8,124-8,127 ft depending on survey source) is the high point on the ridge linking Mount Fernow and Seven Fingered Jack above Entiat Meadows, in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It is NOT a Holden/boat-access peak like its Railroad Creek neighbors — the standard approach is the long Entiat River Trail up the Entiat River valley on the east (Entiat) side of the range, making this primarily a multi-day backpack-and-scramble trip.
beta: The standard line climbs a rib on the south side of the peak directly above Entiat Meadows — parties describe it as the least brushy, straightest option among several parallel ribs/gullies on the south face. Parties gain a broad south/southwest slope of scree, talus, and heather to the summit ridge; in early season this same terrain holds firm snow and the final ridge can be corniced with gendarmes, turning the outing into a real mountaineering objective rather than a summer scramble.

first_pass.evidence: South-side rib and gully from Entiat Meadows to the east ridge at 7,900 ft, a non-technical scramble on scree and heather; no class rating stated
first_pass.note: No source gives a class; kept the top of the record's Class 2-3.
